title: EVERYONE WAS AFRAID OF HIM.
paragraphs: EVERYONE WAS AFRAID OF HIM.

They chained him.
He broke the chains.

They bound his wrists.
He shattered the iron.
He lived where the dead slept — among tombs, under a bruised sky, screaming into caves that echoed his torment.
And here’s the question nobody asked:
What does grace do with a man like that?
Open your Bible to Gospel of Mark 5.

Night air.
Salt from the sea.
A shoreline in the region of the Gerasenes.

The boat door opens.
And Jesus steps out.
Before anyone can speak, a man rushes Him — naked shame, scarred skin, eyes wild with voices that were not his own.
Scripture says he was possessed by an unclean spirit. Not one.
Many.
“My name is Legion, for we are many.”

He wasn’t just troubled.
He was occupied.
Some scholars interpret “Legion” to suggest thousands, echoing a Roman military unit — whether literal or symbolic, the point is clear: this man was overwhelmed beyond human strength.
And yet…
The demons screamed.
Not at the man.
At Jesus.
“Have You come to torment us?”
Pause there.
Hell recognizes authority even when humans don’t.

The townspeople were afraid of the man.
The demons were afraid of Christ.

One word from Jesus.
Permission given.
A herd of pigs rushes down a steep bank — water explodes upward — bodies sink.
Silence.
Now see him.

The man who cut himself with stones…
is sitting.

The man who broke chains…
is still.

The man who howled in darkness…
is clothed.
And in his right mind.
That’s the Gospel in one snapshot.
Let’s be honest.

Some of you don’t live in tombs —
but you live in secrets.

Addictions.
Rage.
Lust.
Bitterness that chains you tighter than iron ever could.

You’ve scared people.
You’ve hurt people.
Maybe you’ve even scared yourself.
But hear me carefully:

Jesus does not negotiate with darkness.
He commands it.
And when Christ restores you, He doesn’t just calm you —
He commissions you.
The healed man begs to go with Jesus.

Let me leave.
Let me escape this town that remembers who I was.
But Jesus says no.
“Go home to your friends and tell them how much the Lord has done for you.”
That’s the twist.

Grace doesn’t always relocate you.
Sometimes it plants you right where your shame was public.
He went home.

Not as a madman.
Not as a threat.
As a testimony.
And the very region that once feared him began to marvel.
Listen to me.
Your worst chapter does not disqualify you from being sent.
It prepares you.
The place that knew your breakdown may be the place that witnesses your breakthrough.

This is not self-help.
This is not positive thinking.
This is resurrection power in real time.
The same Jesus who stepped onto that shore steps into your chaos.

Sin is real.
Bondage is real.
But so is the cross.
At Calvary, Jesus absorbed the full weight of evil — not just to manage it, but to defeat it. His resurrection is the guarantee that no Legion outranks the Lamb.

If you are bound — repent.
If you are ashamed — come.
If you are tired of screaming in internal tombs — kneel.
Grace is not intimidated by your history.
And when Christ makes you whole, go home.
Tell them what He did.
We tell the stories that shame tried to erase.
